query_text: Are there any academic fields that don't have enough people trying to teach?

action.query: 2025 teacher shortage subject areas special education math science foreign language academic fields shortage teachers United States
queries: 2025 teacher shortage subject areas special education math science foreign language academic fields shortage teachers United States
AAEE educator supply and demand report 2025 subject shortage areas teachers

annotations.title: Teacher Shortages by Subjects Across States | Learning Policy Institute

content.text:
Yes—especially in **K–12 teaching**, there are several academic/subject areas where schools often don’t have enough qualified people applying or staying.

In the U.S., the most commonly reported shortage areas are:

- **Special education** — usually the biggest and most persistent shortage.
- **Math**, especially middle/high school.
- **Science**, especially **physics**, **chemistry**, and sometimes general secondary science.
- **Bilingual education / ESL / English learner instruction**.
- **World languages** — Spanish in some places, but also harder-to-fill languages.
- **Career and technical education** — trades, health sciences, computer/IT, agriculture, etc.
- **Rural and high-poverty schools** across many subjects, even where the subject is not nationally scarce.

Recent national shortage data show special education, science, and math as among the most widely reported shortage fields across states; one 2025 Learning Policy Institute update found shortages reported in **45 states for special education**, **41 for science**, and **40 for math**. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-shortages-subjects-across-states-factsheet?utm_source=openai)) The American Association for Employment in Education similarly lists **special education, physics, chemistry, and math** as continuing “considerable shortage” areas. ([aaee.org](https://www.aaee.org/newpagea16258f7?utm_source=openai))

There are also fields where there may be **too many applicants relative to jobs**, depending on location—often **social studies/history**, **elementary education in desirable districts**, and sometimes **English/language arts**. But this varies a lot by state, district, pay, working conditions, and grade level.

If you mean **college/university teaching**, the shortage picture is different: many academic fields have *too many* PhD holders for tenure-track jobs, but there can still be shortages in applied/professional areas like **nursing, computer science, engineering, accounting, special education, and some health fields**, where industry jobs pay much more than academia.
